# Longitudinal associations between bilateral versus unilateral knee osteoarthritis and physical performance measures

**Authors:** Jennifer S Hanberg; Faith Selzer; Elena Losina; Jeffrey N Katz; Jamie E Collins

**Affiliations:** aDivision of Rheumatology, Inflammation and Immunity, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | bDepartment of Orthopedic Surgery, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | cHarvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Bilateral knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is common, but evidence for the effect of bilateral versus unilateral KOA on functional outcomes is conflicting. We aimed to examine the association between bilateral versus unilateral KOA and physical performance measures over two years.

Our cohort included adults with symptomatic, radiographic KOA. Study assessments at baseline, 12 and 24 months included the 30-s chair sit-to-stand task (CST) and 40-m walk (40 ​MW). We defined bilateral KOA as Kellgren-Lawrence grade ≥2 and Knee Osteoarthritis Outcome Pain Scale ≥17/100 in both knees. We used linear mixed models to (1) assess the cross-sectional association between the presence of bilateral versus unilateral KOA at each timepoint and performance measures, and (2) assess the association between bilateral versus unilateral KOA at baseline and longitudinal changes in performance measures. Models were adjusted for clinical and demographic covariates.

101 participants were included. At baseline, 43/101 (43 ​%) had bilateral KOA. In adjusted models, bilateral, versus unilateral, KOA was associated with 1.0 fewer stands on the CST (95 ​% CI: 2.2–0.1), and a 0.03 ​m/s slower 40 ​MW (95 ​% CI: 0.10–0.04). Average 2-year change in CST was −0.6 stands in those with baseline bilateral KOA and −0.7 in those with unilateral KOA (between-group difference, 0.1 stands (95 ​% CI: 1.7–1.8)). The baseline bilateral KOA group had greater worsening in 40 ​MW time (between-group difference −0.10 ​m/s (95 ​% CI: -0.20–0.00)).

We did not find clinically significant associations between bilateral vs unilateral KOA and performance on two physical performance tasks over two years of follow-up in this cohort study.

Keywords: Osteoarthritis, Knee, Bilateral, Physical performance

## Introduction

Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common type of arthritis and is a leading cause of disability and healthcare expenditure in the United States, with OA of the knee occurring in approximately 9 ​% of the US population by the age of 60 [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]. The clinical course of OA is heterogeneous and individualized prognostication is difficult. Given the clinical heterogeneity in OA progression over time, there is a need to develop better tools to predict the progression of OA in individual patients [6,7].

Bilateral involvement occurs in about 1/3 to 2/3 of patients with knee OA (KOA), depending on the population examined [[8], [9], [10]]. Bilateral KOA is of clinical interest due to its association with reduced quality of life and the potential for bilateral joint replacement, and because it could represent a practical and clinically accessible prognostic factor for predicting progression [11]. Previously published definitions of bilateral KOA are heterogeneous, with some authors defining bilateral KOA by the presence of radiographic KOA only [12], others by the presence of both pain and radiographic KOA [10,13], and others [8,14] by bilateral pain with radiographic change on at least one side. Bilateral knee osteoarthritis is more common among individuals with low educational attainment and is associated with higher rates of widespread pain [15,16]. Existing evidence for the clinical importance of prevalent bilateral KOA with respect to symptoms and physical functioning is conflicting. Some studies have reported no difference in pain, walking speed, and gait parameters [2,12,13] while others have found worse chair sit-stand performance, higher pain sensitization, and greater risk for joint replacement among participants with bilateral KOA [8,17,18].

In addition to gaps in knowledge regarding the effect of prevalent bilateral KOA on pain and function, there are also important unanswered questions concerning the longitudinal progression of OARSI-endorsed [19] (Osteoarthritis Research Society International) objective performance measures over time. Existing cross-sectional studies reveal weak correlations between more frequently collected subjective measures (pain, quality of life) and objective, physical performance measures (including chair sit-to-stand performance and walk speed) [16]. Furthermore, although many studies have attempted to describe and quantify trajectories of pain and structural change in KOA [[21], [22], [23], [24], [25]], few studies have reported physical performance measures at multiple timepoints [12,26]. Sharma and colleagues [12] investigated prognostic factors for poor physical function measured by chair-stand performance over 3 years. They found that 66 ​% of participants had a poor outcome on the chair sit-to-stand task, defined as either no change in the quintile of performance if the participant was in the 1st-3rd quintiles at the baseline visit, or worsening in the quintile of performance (e.g., from 2nd to 1st (worst) quintile). Baseline radiographic bilateral knee OA was one of 14 candidate risk factors examined and the authors did not find associations between this and chair stand performance over 3 years. However, 90 ​% of participants had bilateral knee OA at baseline. Baumbach et al. [26] aimed to build high-dimensional models to predict individual changes in several outcomes including 40-m walking speed. Outcomes were measured over just 6 weeks and the authors did not include presence of bilateral disease as a predictor. Additional prospective studies are required to examine longer-term changes in these physical performance outcomes and to assess whether bilateral disease is associated with worsening physical function.

In this investigation, we sought to examine the association between bilateral versus unilateral symptomatic, radiographic knee osteoarthritis and physical performance measures over two years of follow-up in a cohort of patients with KOA. We hypothesized (1) that bilateral (as compared with unilateral) disease is associated with poorer physical performance cross-sectionally, and (2) that participants with bilateral KOA at baseline experience greater worsening in physical performance over two years.

## Methods

Study design and sample: This was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Osteoarthritis Registry of Biomarker and Imaging Trajectories (ORBIT) cohort, which has been described previously [20]. The ORBIT study recruited participants from the Brigham and Women's Hospital Orthopedic and Arthritis Center in Boston, MA between 2018 and 2020. Inclusion criteria included: age ≥40 years, knee pain for >4 weeks, prior radiograph with Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) grade 2 or 3 KOA of either knee within 2 years of screening, fluency in English, and a modified Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) pain score ≥2/12. To calculate the modified KOOS score, participants were asked to rate their level of pain in the more bothersome knee while walking on flat surfaces, walking up or down stairs, and standing upright, with each question scored from 0 (no pain) to 4 (extreme pain); a score of at least 2/12 was specified as a minimum pain threshold for inclusion in the ORBIT study; i.e., at least mild pain on two of three items or moderate pain on one item. Exclusion criteria were: prior radiograph with K-L grade 4 disease in either knee, planned knee replacement within 1 year, prior knee replacement, inflammatory arthritis, neurological conditions precluding questionnaire completion, pregnancy, nursing home residence, contraindication to MRI, unwillingness to provide blood specimen, or receipt of Worker's Compensation.

Participants were followed over 48 months, with study visits at baseline, 12, and 24 months incorporating physical performance measures, questionnaires, and imaging, including standing bilateral radiographs. Follow-up questionnaires were administered at 48 months. Measurements were carried out by trained and certified research staff.

Exposures: Our primary exposure of interest was bilateral, compared to unilateral, KOA. We defined bilateral KOA as (1) the presence of K-L grade 2 or higher on bilateral knee radiographs and (2) the presence of pain in both knees, defined as a score ≥17/100 on the full KOOS Pain Scale. This threshold is similar to the study inclusion criterion: mild pain on greater than 2/3 of KOOS Pain items or moderate pain on greater than 1/3 of KOOS Pain items. Subjects who did not fulfill both of these criteria were labeled as having unilateral KOA. We assessed the presence of bilateral KOA at each timepoint. Our primary analyses included all participants. In secondary analysis, we excluded participants whose bilateral vs. unilateral status changed over time.

Outcomes: The primary outcome was performance on the 30-s chair sit-to-stand task [19]. This test measures the number of times a participant can complete a full transfer of weight from sitting to standing within 30 ​s. The secondary outcome was walking speed on the 40-m walk task, which assesses the amount of time it takes for a participant to walk a 10-m distance four consecutive times at their fastest walking pace. Both measures are part of the set of tests recommended by OARSI to assess physical function in people diagnosed with hip or knee OA [19]. The 30-s chair sit-to-stand task was chosen as the primary outcome based on prior findings from Riddle and Stratford, who identified that performance on the chair sit-to-stand task, but not the 20-m walk, was associated with bilateral versus unilateral knee pain in a cohort of participants with radiographic KOA in at least one knee [8]. 40-m walk speed was chosen as the secondary outcome due to its relevance to performance in daily life, understanding that it is also influenced by non-musculoskeletal factors such as cardiopulmonary disease. Participants completed the KOOS Pain and Quality of Life (0–100, 100 worst) questionnaire at each visit. We assessed the outcomes as continuous measures and also dichotomized changes over time as worsening by the minimally clinically important difference (MCID) or greater. The MCID thresholds were 2.6 stands and 0.3 ​m/s for the 30-s chair sit-to-stand and 40-m walk, and 8 points out of 100 for KOOS Pain and Quality of Life [27,28]. Outcomes measured after a knee replacement were excluded from analyses.

Covariates: We determined a priori that several clinical covariates might confound the observed association between bilateral vs unilateral knee OA and physical performance outcomes. These included age, sex, baseline duration of pain in the more bothersome knee (2 years or more versus <2 years), education (associate's degree or higher versus some college or less), body mass index, widespread pain (assessed via a modified Widespread Pain Index, with knee scores omitted), and the use of therapeutic injections within 3 months prior to each measurement of physical performance (reported by the participant). Age and duration of pain were chosen as covariates due to the higher likelihood of developing bilateral symptoms with time, while education may be associated with occupational exposures that increase the risk of injury and unilateral OA. The widespread pain index was hypothesized to be associated with risk of diffuse pain and therefore a higher likelihood of reporting bilateral knee pain, and the presence of injections was included as a covariate as it may influence the presence of pain at the time of questionnaire (and hence classification of a participant as having bilateral versus unilateral knee KOA).

We also calculated the baseline Charlson Comorbidity Index, which was reported as a variable of interest and used for multiple imputation but not expected to be a confounder of the primary exposure-outcome relationship [29]. A history of knee injury was assessed by questionnaire, indicating whether the participant had ever sustained a knee injury that caused difficulty walking for at least one week.

Ethics Approval: The ORBIT study was approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board.

Statistical Analysis: For categorical variables, we calculated and reported frequencies and percentages, and for continuous variables, we assessed measures of central tendency and spread as either mean (standard deviation) or median (25th-75th percentile) as appropriate.

We used linear mixed modeling to assess the bivariable and multivariable-adjusted relationship between bilateral (vs. unilateral) symptomatic and radiographic KOA and the outcomes of interest. The primary exposure and covariates were considered as fixed effects, with each individual participant included as a random effect to account for repeated measures over time. All analyses included up to three timepoints per participant.

The first set of analyses examined the cross-sectional association between the presence of bilateral disease and physical performance, assessed at each visit. Covariates in the multivariable model included study visit, age, sex, education, BMI, baseline duration of pain, the baseline modified widespread pain, and the presence of therapeutic injection in either knee within 3 months prior to a given study visit.

The second hypothesis addressed whether the presence of bilateral disease at baseline was associated with a faster rate of worsening physical performance over time. For this set of analyses, the presence of bilateral disease was defined at baseline and we added an interaction term between time and the baseline bilateral indicator variable. In the primary analysis, we only considered baseline bilateral disease status.

In pre-specified sensitivity analyses for both hypotheses, we excluded participants whose bilateral vs. unilateral status changed over time.

Missing data: Linear mixed effects models are robust to data missing at random (MAR) [30]. However, given the relatively high frequency of missing follow-up data, we performed several sensitivity analyses, including multiple imputation of missing outcomes by chained equations, to assess the potential bias due to non-random missing data on our primary findings [31]. The imputation model included age, sex, BMI, modified widespread pain scores, education level, the Charlson comorbidity index, and an indicator for bilateral KOA at baseline. We also imputed missing covariates (education level, presence of bilateral vs nonbilateral disease at follow-up visits, and history of joint injection within 3 months prior to missed follow-up visits). We considered a variety of scenarios under both the MAR and missing not at random (MNAR) assumptions. Under the MAR assumption, we assume that missing outcomes can be imputed from observed outcomes and covariates; under MNAR we assume that actual outcomes may differ from those imputed based on observed data alone [32]. We used a tipping point approach in MNAR sensitivity analyses, imputing missing outcomes under a range of assumptions to determine how severe the missing data imbalance must be to change our conclusions. We ranged imputed data between ±2 standard deviations higher or lower than was predicted based on observed outcomes and covariates alone, including scenarios where imputed data was higher/lower than predicted for all participants with missing data, for participants with bilateral KOA only, and for participants with unilateral KOA only. We generated 20 imputed datasets and combined the results using Rubin's rules [31].

Statistical significance was defined as a two-tailed p-value of <0.05. We performed the analyses in SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC) and R version 4.4.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with RStudio version 2024.04.2 (Posit Software).

## Results

The study included 101 participants who completed a baseline visit, of whom 72 and 62 completed the primary outcome assessment at the 12- and 24-month follow-up visits (Table 1). Details of cohort assembly are reported in Fig. S1. The mean age was 64 years and 63 ​% of patients were female. At baseline, 43 ​% of participants were categorized as having bilateral KOA. Participants with bilateral KOA at baseline were on average 3 years younger than those in the unilateral group (62 years compared to 65 years), and 33/41 (80 ​%) had a body mass index of at least 25 ​kg/m2 compared to 43/57 (75 ​%) in the unilateral group (Table 1). The distribution of sex and educational level was similar between groups (Table 1). A history of knee injury was present in 44 ​% (N ​= ​19) of patients with bilateral OA at baseline, compared to 59 ​% (N ​= ​34) of patients with unilateral OA. Median modified widespread pain index score (omitting pain in the knees) was 4 [25th-75th percentile, 3–8] in the unilateral group and 3 [2–5] in the bilateral group, with the quartiles suggesting substantial overlap in the distribution between groups. While most participants with bilateral or unilateral KOA at baseline remained in the same category throughout follow-up, 22 participants (22 ​%) met criteria for both bilateral and unilateral KOA at different times during the study. 10 of 43 participants classified as bilateral at baseline did not meet the criteria for bilateral KOA at one or more subsequent timepoints, and 22 of 58 participants classified as unilateral at baseline did meet the criteria for bilateral KOA at one or more subsequent timepoints.

### Cross-sectional between-group differences

Chair sit-to-stand performance was similar between the groups at each visit (Fig. 1). At baseline, the median number of stands was 11 (25th-75th percentile, 9–13) in the group with bilateral KOA compared to 12 (9–15) among those classified as having unilateral KOA. At 24 months the median number of stands was 11 in both groups (Table 2). The 40-m walk speed was similar between groups at baseline (mean 1.5 (0.4) m/s vs. 1.5 (0.3) m/s) and at the 12- and 24-month visits (Table 2). KOOS pain and quality-of-life scores were worse at all 3 timepoints among participants with bilateral vs. unilateral KOA (Table 2).

## Discussion

In this prospective cohort study, we did not find that the presence of bilateral, compared to unilateral, symptomatic and radiographic knee osteoarthritis was associated with worse physical performance on the 30-s chair sit-to-stand or 40-m walk. We also did not find that participants with bilateral compared to unilateral KOA worsened faster with respect to physical performance measurements over two years of follow-up.

Few studies have examined physical performance measures specifically among persons with bilateral vs. unilateral KOA. Messier and colleagues [13] did not find differences in kinetic and kinematic parameters, such as stride length, support time, and hip and knee forces, among participants with bilateral symptomatic and radiographic KOA, but did not specifically examine physical performance tests. White et al. [33] examined questionnaire-based measures of physical functioning and reported that both low physical function at baseline, and improvement in function over follow-up, were more common in participants with unilateral than bilateral pain. Riddle and Stratford [8] found that bilateral KOA with severe pain in at least one knee was associated with a worse chair sit-to-stand performance (adjusted between-group difference of 0.06–0.09 stands per second, or 1.8 to 2.7 stands per 30 ​s); this difference was not observed in participants reporting mild or moderate pain in both knees, and was not observed for the outcome of 20-m walk speed [8]. Our estimated between-group difference in the primary analysis of 1.0 stands was smaller than this, but the effect size among participants with consistently bilateral or consistently unilateral KOA was of a similar magnitude to the result reported by Riddle and Stratford. Additionally, our cohort included a higher proportion of female participants (63 ​% versus 50 ​%) than that reported by Riddle and Stratford, and included participants with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2 or higher radiographic KOA (versus 3 or higher in Riddle and Stratford's cohort). It is possible that the exclusion of participants with milder radiographic KOA in the Riddle and Stratford study may have led to greater observed between-group differences.

Our study adds to the existing literature with a longitudinal modeling approach that quantifies the association between bilateral disease and objective physical performance measurements over time. We found that neither chair sit-to-stand performance nor 40-m walk speed was associated with bilateral versus unilateral KOA status, and estimated between-group differences did not approach MCIDs in the primary analysis [27]. We also observed that performance on both the chair sit-to-stand and 40-m walk was overall stable over 2 years, with the vast majority of participants exhibiting change less than the test-specific MCID. These data advance our understanding of the prognosis of KOA-related physical function impairment – namely, that performance is unlikely to decrease in a clinically important fashion over 2 years of follow-up, and that the presence of bilateral versus unilateral KOA at baseline or at any given timepoint is not a poor prognostic marker for such outcomes. Therefore, future risk prediction tools may not need to incorporate the presence of bilateral or unilateral KOA as a risk factor for worsening physical function.

Of note, worsening by the MCID in chair sit-to-stand performance was numerically more common among participants with unilateral disease, while worsening in walk speed was more common among participants with bilateral KOA, although these differences were not statistically significant and these results, which are based on study completers, should be interpreted with caution. Multivariable adjusted models including all participants did not identify bilaterality as a correlate of these differences, suggesting the observed unadjusted between-group difference may be due to confounding (such as by BMI, education, or other demographic and clinical factors) or missing data. In light of these results, participants with symptomatic, radiographic bilateral KOA that have not progressed to K-L grade 4 may be counseled that their physical performance is unlikely to worsen dramatically over the next two years.

There is no universally accepted definition for bilateral KOA, with some author groups defining bilateral disease by the presence of symptoms only (in the context of radiographic disease in at least one knee), [8,33] versus radiographic KOA only [12], versus both symptoms and radiographic KOA. [10,17,13] We chose to evaluate bilateral KOA by the presence of both structural KOA (K-L grade ≥2) and symptoms in both knees, as the absence of bilateral structural KOA in a participant with bilateral pain suggests a different mechanism, such as central sensitization, for bilateral pain.

Our study has several strengths. The ORBIT cohort is clinically well-characterized and importantly collected data concerning longitudinal change in physical performance measurements, which are described less frequently than subjective outcomes in the existing literature [20,34]. This investigation also has certain limitations. Participants were recruited from a single academic referral center, and this may limit generalizability. There was a high rate of loss to follow-up in this cohort likely due to the COVID-19 pandemic; however, we used multiple imputation methods to better understand the worst-case scenarios for missing data and confirmed that for our primary findings to change, missingness not-at-random would need to be present with a between-group difference of more than one standard deviation. While model diagnostics were overall reassuring against gross violations of key assumptions, we have used linear modeling for the primary outcome of chair sit-to-stand, which is most accurately described as a count variable. Fourth, while our definition of bilateral KOA is clinically relevant, incorporating both structural change and symptoms, it does allow participants to change from bilateral to unilateral over time if pain improves; this reduces the stability of classification within an individual participant over time. Additionally, this study observed participants over a course of two years, while progression in OA is often seen over longer time periods. Future analyses may evaluate these associations in additional data sources with larger sample sizes and/or longer follow-up. Finally, the relatively small sample size and loss-to-follow-up limit our power to detect interactions in the primary analysis, or to undertake sex-stratified analyses.

In summary, we did not observe a clinically significant association between bilateral vs unilateral KOA with performance on two physical function tasks over two years of follow-up. Future studies may investigate the associations between bilateral KOA and objective and subjective function measures over longer time periods.

## Abstract

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common respiratory viral illness which can cause severe outcomes in older and immunosuppressed populations. There is little data regarding RSV outcomes among people with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs).

This retrospective cohort study examined risk factors for hospitalization in individuals with SARDs and documented RSV infection between 2015 and 2023 at Mass General Brigham (Boston, MA). Clinical data were collected from electronic health records. Multivariable adjusted logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with hospitalization for RSV infection.

Of 188 individuals with SARDs and RSV (mean age 68.5 years, 75.5% female), 96 (51.0%) were hospitalized. Higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (aOR 1.16 per point, 95% CI: 1.04–1.31), Claims-Based Frailty Index (aOR 4.80 vs. robust/pre-frail, 95% CI: 2.32–9.94), and concurrent infection (aOR 2.52 vs. RSV alone, 95% CI: 1.07–5.92) were associated with increased odds of hospitalization. CD20 inhibitor treatment (aOR 3.84 vs. csDMARD, 95% CI: 0.99–15.20) and older age (OR 1.03 per year, 95% CI: 1.01–1.05) were associated with numerically increased odds of RSV hospitalization. Among hospitalized individuals, 56% required oxygen. There were 12 deaths within 90 days (12.5% of those hospitalized; 6% of all with RSV).

This study highlights the increased risk of severe outcomes of RSV infection in individuals with SARDs. Factors associated with RSV hospitalization included frailty, higher comorbidity burden, and concurrent infection at the time of RSV. These findings should inform clinical decisions regarding RSV vaccination and prevention strategies.

## Introduction

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common viral infection that usually affects the upper respiratory tract. While RSV infection most often causes mild illness in the general adult population, it can cause severe respiratory illness, particularly in elderly and high-risk adults [1]. Data from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) between 2016 and 2023 estimates rates of RSV-associated hospitalization in the United States between 48.9 to 76.2 per 100,000 adults per season [2]. RSV-associated hospitalizations are overall less common than hospitalizations due to COVID-19 or influenza. However, prior to the availability of RSV vaccines in 2023, people with RSV experienced similar severe infection outcomes compared to those with COVID-19 or influenza among those not vaccinated for these viruses, and RSV outcomes were more severe than COVID-19 or influenza among vaccinated individuals [3]. Increased risk of worse RSV outcomes including hospitalization and mortality have been noted in individuals with a history of hematologic malignancies [4], hematopoietic stem cell transplantation [4,5], and solid organ transplantation [6,7]. Our understanding of other factors impacting RSV-related complications and death, however, particularly among individuals with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) remains limited.

This is of particular concern as individuals with SARDs may be at increased risk of severe infection due to the intrinsic pathobiology of the systemic disease as well as use of immunosuppressive treatment [8]. Thus, current guidelines for individuals with SARDs recommend routine vaccinations for vaccine-preventable respiratory diseases including influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal pneumonia, and others; the most recent American College of Rheumatology SARD vaccination guideline was published in 2022, prior to the approval of the RSV vaccine in the United States [13].

The approval of the first RSV vaccine in 2023 further emphasizes the need to understand risk factors for severe RSV infection to determine which populations would most benefit from vaccination. Three different RSV vaccines (Arexvy from GlaxoSmithKline [14], Abrysvo from Pfizer [15], and mRESVIA from Moderna [16]) are currently available in the US, and the CDC’s current recommendation is for RSV vaccination for all adults aged 75 years and older and for those aged 50–74 who are at increased risk of severe RSV [17].

There is currently little data regarding RSV outcomes among those with SARDs, particularly in relation to the associations of different disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). The objective of this study was to evaluate the risk of severe outcomes of RSV infections in individuals with SARDs and to identify risk factors for hospitalization during RSV infections within this population. We performed this study in the period prior to widespread availability of RSV vaccination.

## Methods

### Study design, participants, and exposures

We performed a retrospective cohort study investigating factors associated with hospitalization during RSV infection among individuals with SARDs in a large healthcare system. Mass General Brigham (MGB) is a multi-center healthcare system that includes a total of 14 hospitals, including two tertiary care hospitals (Massachusetts General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital), as well as other primary care and specialty outpatient centers in the greater Boston, Massachusetts, US area. We initially identified individuals who had both a positive laboratory test (either Polymerase Chain Reaction or antigen testing) for RSV in the outpatient setting, emergency department, or inpatient setting at MGB between June 1, 2015, and November 30, 2023, and any ICD-10 code for any SARD. Then, we performed manual electronic health record (EHR) review to confirm SARD diagnoses as well as the specific SARD type. The index date was the first RSV positive laboratory test among each patient with a prevalent SARD. This study was approved by the MGB Institutional Review Board (2020P000833).

### Outcomes assessment

We performed a manual review of each individual’s EHR to ascertain clinical outcomes including RSV symptoms, hospitalization status, medical interventions, and death. RSV hospitalization was defined as admission to a hospital within 10 days of a positive RSV test and mortality was defined as death within 90 days of positive RSV test. Concurrent bacterial pneumonia was defined as confirmed and/or suspected pneumonia, based on at least any one of: 1) radiographic infiltrate consistent with pneumonia, 2) microbiological (e.g., sputum sample, bronchoalveolar lavage) evidence, and/or 3) treatment with antibiotics. Cause of death was obtained from review of the EHR (e.g., death certificate, relevant notes).

### Covariates of interest

We used electronic query to extract variables including demographics (e.g., age at index date of RSV infection, sex, race, ethnicity, Claims-Based Frailty Index [CFI], Charlson Comorbidity Index [CCI]) and clinical values (e.g., body mass index [BMI], estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] and hemoglobin A1c [Hgb A1c]). The CFI is a validated claims-based index which categorizes frailty on a deficit-accumulation model, categorizing individuals as robust (CFI <0.15), prefrail (0.15–0.24), or frail (>0.25) [18]. The CCI is a summary measure that incorporates a variety of different potential comorbidities and predicts 10-year survival [19]. We manually reviewed the EHR to collect other exposures of interest (e.g., SARD diagnosis and treatment, individual comorbidities, and concurrent infections). For analyses involving DMARD treatment, individuals were categorized into the following mutually exclusive hierarchical groups: no DMARD, conventional synthetic DMARD (csDMARD), targeted synthetic DMARD, TNF inhibitor, CD20 inhibitor, or other biologic DMARD (bDMARD), with the biologic taking precedence in those on multiple medications.

### Statistical analysis

We evaluated the association of baseline factors, including demographics, SARD diagnosis and treatment, comorbidities, frailty, and concurrent infections, with hospitalization during RSV infection. We used unadjusted and multivariable logistic regression to assess the association of these baseline factors with the odds of hospitalization during RSV infection. Multivariable analyses were adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, CCI, and CFI. To assess the robustness of our results, we performed a subgroup analysis in which we limited the population to those with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or other forms of inflammatory arthritis. We also performed a secondary analysis with an outcome of hospitalization due to RSV infection. The level of significance was set as a two-tailed p < 0.05, and statistical analyses were conducted using SAS statistical software (version 9.4; SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC).

### Factors associated with hospitalization during RSV infection

Among 188 people with a SARD and RSV infection, 96 (51 %) were hospitalized during their RSV infection (Table 1). The mean age of those hospitalized during RSV infection was 72 years compared with 66 years for non-hospitalized individuals (p < 0.01) (Table 1). Older age had significantly higher odds of RSV hospitalization in unadjusted analyses (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.03 per year, 95 % CI [1.01–1.05]), and numerically higher risk in multivariable analyses (multivariable adjusted odds ratio [aOR] of 1.02 per year, 95 % CI: 0.996–1.04). Higher CCI (aOR 1.16 per point, 95 % CI: 1.04–1.31), frailty by CFI (aOR 4.80 vs. robust/pre-frail, 95 % CI: 2.32–9.94), and concurrent infection (aOR 2.52 vs. RSV alone, 95 % CI: 1.07–5.92) were associated with increased odds of hospitalization (Fig. 1; Supplementary Table 1). Of the immunosuppressive medications evaluated, treatment with a CD20 inhibitor in the 12 months prior to RSV infection was associated with numerically higher odds of hospitalization (aOR 3.84 vs. csDMARD use, 95 % CI: 0.99–15.20).

### RA and inflammatory arthritis subgroup analysis

A subgroup analysis was performed among individuals with RA or other inflammatory arthritis (n = 98) (Supplementary Tables 3–4). Similar to the overall cohort, frailty (aOR 5.15 vs. robust/pre-frail, 95 % CI: 1.78–14.87) was associated with significantly increased odds of hospitalization. In this cohort, age, concurrent bacterial pneumonia, and lower eGFR were numerically but not significantly associated with higher odds of hospitalization.

### In-hospital interventions and deaths for individuals with SARDs during RSV infection

Of the 96 individuals hospitalized during RSV infection, 84 % were for RSV or infection-related complications and 56 % required varying levels of oxygen support (Table 2). The greatest proportion of those requiring support required nasal cannula oxygen (40 %), and a minority required high-flow or non-invasive ventilation (including continuous or bilevel positive airway pressure) (8 %), invasive mechanical ventilation (7 %), or extracorporeal membrane support (ECMO) (1 %). Within 30 days of hospital discharge, 26 % of hospitalized individuals were readmitted. Of all individuals with RSV infection, 12 individuals (6 %) died within 90 days of RSV infection and 7 of these deaths (58 %) were attributed to RSV (Supplementary Table 5). The individuals who died within 90 days of RSV infection were older than those in the overall cohort (mean age of 79 years); three individuals were between ages 60 and 75 and the remaining nine were older than age 75. Half of those who died were receiving treatment with a csDMARD or bDMARD for their SARD; the other half were not using any DMARD. Eleven of the twelve (92 %) had pre-existing cardiovascular and/or pulmonary comorbidities at or prior to RSV infection, and 4 (33 %) had moderate to severe chronic kidney disease.

## Discussion

In this retrospective multicenter study, we evaluated clinical outcomes of individuals with SARDs and RSV infection within a large, multi-institutional healthcare system in the United States and identified factors associated with increased risk of being hospitalized during RSV infection. This is the first study to investigate the characteristics and outcomes of individuals with SARDs and RSV infection. We found that frailty, concurrent infection, and greater overall comorbidity burden were associated with increased odds of hospitalization during RSV infection and that higher eGFR was associated with lower odds of hospitalization. Older age and use of CD20 inhibitors were associated with numerically higher odds of hospitalization in multivariable analyses. For individuals who required hospitalization during RSV infection, over half required some level of oxygen report. Twelve individuals (6 % of those overall with infection and 12.5 % of those hospitalized) died within 90 days of infection of all causes, 7 of which were directly attributable to RSV infection. Of those who died, the average age was 10 years older than that of the overall cohort of those with SARDs and RSV infection, and most had cardiovascular and/or pulmonary comorbidities at the time of RSV infection. Thus, individuals with SARDs are at risk of poor RSV infection outcomes, supporting current recommendations for RSV vaccination in this vulnerable group.

Our finding of older age being associated with higher odds of hospitalization on univariable analysis and in multivariable analysis with the outcome of hospitalization due to RSV infection is consistent with prior studies investigating RSV in the adult population. Older age (>75 and >85 years) has been described in the general population as a factor for more severe RSV disease and RSV-related mortality [20,21]. Older adults have greater risk of complications from numerous infections including viral respiratory illnesses and bacterial pneumonias due to age-related changes in both innate and adaptive immune responses, creating an imbalance between chronic low-level inflammation and reduced adaptive immune efficacy to pathogenic targets [22,23]. We also found frailty, another age-associated factor but distinct from chronological age, to be significantly associated with increased odds of hospitalization both during and due to RSV infection. Age was not associated with significantly higher odds of hospitalization in multi-variable analyses, though our multivariable analysis was adjusted for CFI, among other factors. Autoimmune disease is a risk factor for the onset of frailty and frailty itself is a risk factor for adverse outcomes for individuals with rheumatologic disease [24]. Frailty has been independently associated with serious outcomes and mortality in other SARDs, including rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis [25,26].

Greater comorbidity burden was another factor that was associated with increased odds of hospitalization, with this study demonstrating that those hospitalized had lower eGFRs and higher CCI score (reflecting total burden of comorbidity) than those not hospitalized. Of the 12 individuals who died within 90 days of RSV infection, 11 had substantial pre-existing cardiopulmonary morbidities including heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), ILD, asthma, and pulmonary malignancy, reflecting the impact that non-SARD diagnoses have in contributing to adverse outcomes from RSV infection. The impact of pre-existing diseases on worse RSV outcomes has also been seen in other studies of the general population, with cardiorespiratory disease and obesity identified as risk factors for ICU admission among individuals hospitalized for RSV. Pre-existing pulmonary (e.g., from underlying COPD, ILD, asthma) and cardiac disease were identified as risk factors for intubation [21,27]. This has particular relevance to those with SARDs as these individuals are at increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease compared to the general population [28] and many SARDs can cause renal involvement and subsequent progressive renal damage [29]. ILD can be a significant complication in a wide range of SARDs, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, and myositis, with a wide range in prevalence estimates between countries and healthcare settings [30]. In this study, there were significantly more individuals with ILD who were hospitalized but this significance was lost in the multivariable analysis, likely related to sample size (only 23 with ILD).

The impact of immunosuppressive medications on increased risk of severe infection due to RSV remains an area of active investigation. A prior study looking broadly at immunocompromised people with RSV found that those treated with chronic immunosuppressive medications were more likely to require hospitalization but only included 20 total adult participants being treated and did not differentiate between different categories of immunosuppressive medications [31]. Additionally, immunocompromised individuals have been shown to have a heterogenous and often reduced antibody response to the new RSV vaccine, with up to 40 % of participants having inadequate antibody responses at 4 weeks post-vaccination, substantially lower than that reported in the immunocompetent population [32,33]. We found that treatment with CD20 inhibitors was associated with numerically increased odds of hospitalization (aOR 3.84, 95 % CI: 0.99–15.20) but did not find significant associations between glucocorticoids (either low-dose or higher doses) or TNF inhibitors and hospitalization. The confidence interval for TNF inhibitors was quite wide, and the numerically increased odds in those not receiving DMARDs may be due to confounding by indication, with individuals who are older, frailer, or have higher comorbidity burden—all factors associated with increased risk of hospitalization—being unable to tolerate or having contraindications to DMARDs. Some individuals in this group may be receiving glucocorticoid monotherapy, possibly at higher doses given the lack of steroid-sparing DMARD, which may also increase risk. CD20 inhibitors have been shown to significantly increase the risk of serious infections, including viral respiratory infections and lower respiratory tract infections such as pneumonia; however, older age and longer duration of underlying SARD among those treated with CD20 inhibitors may also partially explain the results [34,35]. In those with inflammatory bowel disease, systemic glucocorticoids were associated with increased risk of hospitalization [36].

Research in other respiratory viruses has evaluated both vaccine safety as well as outcomes and relationship to viremia. Risks of severe outcomes in individuals with influenza and COVID-19 infections are higher in those with SARDs than in those in the general population [9–11]. Reassuringly, studies on COVID-19 vaccination have demonstrated a reassuring safety profile in the SARD patient population, including in those on DMARDs. Despite possible impaired responses, most individuals generally achieve adequate humoral responses to vaccination as well as evidence of clinical efficacy with decreased rates of hospitalization following vaccination [12]. Studies on other viral infections such as COVID-19 have also found a correlation between the presence and duration of RSV viremia with severe outcomes [37–39]. While this retrospective study did not evaluate RSV viral levels, the relationship between inability to clear the virus due to either the SARD or its treatment and severe outcomes including hospitalization should be an area of future investigation.

Of the 188 SARD individuals with positive RSV tests included in this study, 54 % were hospitalized. This percentage is notably higher than those in other population-level and disease-specific studies of RSV. Studies of adults who initially tested positive for RSV in the outpatient setting estimate that between 5–7 % of individuals overall or 7–9 % of “higher risk” individuals (defined as those ≥65 years or those with asthma, COPD, or congestive heart failure) were hospitalized within 30 days of testing [40,41]. Reasons for the discrepancy between the higher rate of hospitalization in this study compared to others may relate to ascertainment bias, as we identified people with confirmed positive tests within our healthcare system or may relate to additional risks in the setting of SARD diagnoses and immunosuppression. The results of this study on individuals with SARDs are comparable to a similar study which looked at outcomes of people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) with RSV infection, where 45.4 % of those with IBD required hospitalization [36].

Our study has several strengths. First, we systematically identified individuals with SARDs from the entire MGB EHR and manually confirmed all diagnoses. Second, we identified test-confirmed RSV infections using data from the EHR. Third, details regarding comorbidities and medications—particularly immunomodulatory and immunosuppressive medications—prescribed at the time of RSV infection were available. Fourth, we manually reviewed all cases and were able to ascertain detailed information regarding hospitalization, if pertinent, relation to RSV, and causes of death.

Our study also has several limitations. First, we only captured individuals who tested positive for RSV and thus did not identify individuals with either asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic RSV infection who were not tested or who did not present to clinical attention. As RSV testing outside of a healthcare facility is limited and home tests are uncommon, our denominator of individuals with RSV infection is certainly an underestimate, and the absolute proportion with hospitalization and/or death represent overestimates. This is further supported by the fact that our study only had 5 total patients who were classified as robust by the CFI, all of whom were not hospitalized, supportive of this study capturing an overall more frail population that was more likely to have significantly symptomatic or severe RSV infection leading to testing. Second, we did not collect detailed information about rheumatic disease activity or SARD medication interruption around the time of RSV infection which could have potentially impacted results. Third, sample size limited the number of people captured in the different DMARD treatment categories and in those receiving higher doses of glucocorticoids, likely limiting our study’s ability to detect statistical significance. Fourth, the population only includes people with SARDs and thus does not allow for any comparison of outcomes between those with SARDs and the general population. Fifth, while we assessed the first RSV infection for each individual within our study period, we did not have data on RSV infection prior to the study period and thus were not able to assess differences in outcomes between those with a first versus second RSV infection. Sixth, we were not able to assess whether underlying cardiovascular disease (present in 23.9 % of our study population at baseline) was exacerbated following RSV infection. Finally, in defining presence of a concurrent bacterial or fungal pneumonia, we used a broad definition including radiographic or microbiological evidence of disease as well as the treating team’s clinical diagnosis, which risks over-estimating the prevalence of concurrent infection.

## Conclusions

Clinicians who take care of people with SARDs should consider these findings when discussing and recommending age-appropriate RSV vaccination with their patients and when reviewing related prevention strategies such as pneumococcal, COVID-19, and influenza vaccinations, particularly as concurrent infections were associated with increased odds of requiring hospitalization in the setting of RSV infection.

## ABSTRACT

Objectives: To investigate COVID-19 breakthrough infection after third mRNA vaccine dose

among patients with RA by immunomodulator drug class, and we hypothesized that CD20

inhibitors (CD20i) would have higher risk for breakthrough COVID-19 vs. TNF inhibitors (TNFi).

Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study investigating breakthrough COVID-19

among RA patients at Mass General Brigham in Boston, MA, USA. Patients were followed from

the date of 3rd vaccine dose until breakthrough COVID-19, death, or end of follow-up

(18/Jan/2023). Covariates included demographics, lifestyle, comorbidities, and prior COVID-19.

We used Cox proportional hazards models to estimate breakthrough COVID-19 risk by

immunomodulator drug class. We used propensity score (PS) overlap-weighting to compare

users of CD20i vs. TNFi.

Results: We analyzed 5781 patients with RA that received 3 mRNA vaccine doses (78.8%

female, mean age 64.2 years). During mean follow-up of 12.8 months, 1173 (20.2%) had

breakthrough COVID_19. Use of CD20i (adjusted HR 1.74, 95%CI 1.30-2.33) and

glucocorticoid monotherapy (adjusted HR 1.47, 95%CI 1.09-1.98) were each associated with

breakthrough COVID-19 compared to TNFi use. In the PS overlap-weighted analysis, CD20i

users also had higher breakthrough COVID-19 risk than TNFi users (HR 1.62, 95%CI 1.02-

2.56). A sensitivity analysis excluding patients with cancer or interstitial lung disease yielded

similar findings.

Conclusions: We identified CD20i and glucocorticoid monotherapy as risk factors for

breakthrough COVID-19 among patients with RA after a 3rd vaccine dose. This contemporary

study highlights the real-world impact of blunted immune responses in these subgroups and the

need for effective risk mitigation strategies.

## INTRODUCTION

In August 2021, the CDC recommended a third SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine to

complete the initial vaccine series for immunosuppressed patients who had previously received

two mRNA doses1. Thus, many previous studies of breakthrough infection were performed

using a 2-dose definition rather than the contemporary definition of 3 doses. Even after

completing the initial vaccine series, some patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain at

increased risk for breakthrough COVID-19 infection2,3 due to altered underlying immunity and

use of immunomodulators which may lead to blunted immune responses to vaccination and

infection4. Many immunomodulators, especially CD20 inhibitors (CD20i) and glucocorticoids,

have been shown to decrease humoral responses to COVID-19 vaccines4–8, but may not affect

T cell responses to the same extent6,9. As effective protection against infection can be difficult to

predict from immune measurements alone, there is a need for well controlled studies to

understand the contribution of individual immunomodulators to the risk of disease.

Previous studies of breakthrough COVID-19 in patients with systemic autoimmune

diseases (SARDs) have some limitations. A retrospective cohort study2 investigated

breakthrough infection and severity of infection after two mRNA doses, and found that patients

with RA were at higher risk of breakthrough infection compared to patients without RA. Another

study10 found that patients with rheumatic disease who had good vaccine responses by

antibody titer after 2 vaccine doses had lower rates of breakthrough infections than inadequate

or non-responders. Boekel et al., Lancet Rheum 202211 found that patients on

immunosuppressants had similar risk of breakthrough infection compared to those not on

immunosuppressants, and found that seroconversion after vaccination was protective against

breakthrough infection.  Existing studies investigated small or heterogeneous cohorts10,12–14, did

not have data by specific SARD diagnoses15, investigated lower numbers of COVID-19

vaccinations2,3,16,17, or did not compare immunosuppressant classes2,3.

## METHODS

Study design and population

We performed a retrospective cohort study investigating immunomodulatory medications

and risk of breakthrough infection after initial vaccine series (i.e., 3 mRNA vaccine doses)

among patients with RA at Mass General Brigham (MGB). MGB is a multi-center healthcare

system that includes a total of 14 hospitals, including two tertiary care hospitals (Massachusetts

General Hospital and Brigham and Women’s Hospital), as well as other primary care and

specialty outpatient centers in the greater Boston, Massachusetts area.

All patients included had RA, were taking at least one immunomodulatory medication,

and had received at least three mRNA vaccine doses (Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2 or Moderna

mRNA-1273) between 1/Feb/2021 and 6/Jul/2022. The end of follow-up was 18/Jan/2023. We

restricted the analysis to residents of Massachusetts because of state laws mandating vaccine

reporting. Recipients of the Janssen/Johnson and Johnson vaccine were excluded since this

was infrequent and no longer recommended. The index date was the date of 3rd vaccine

receipt. This study was approved by the MGB Institutional Review Board.

Identification of patients with RA

residents, had at least 2 ICD codes for RA within 2 years before initial COVID-19 vaccine dose,

who reported positive testing either at home (such as patients who notified a clinician about a

a patient with COVID-19 infection transferred from an outside hospital). As a secondary

## RESULTS

Study sample and baseline characteristics

We included 5781 patients with RA that received at least 3 mRNA vaccine doses (Table

1, Supplemental Figure 1). A total of 1173 (20.3%) had COVID-19 after the index date (date of

third vaccination). A total of 4311 (74.6%) patients used csDMARDs, 2470 (42.7%) used

biologic DMARDs [including 1727 (29.9%) on TNFi and 172 (3.0%) on CD20i], 490 (8.5%) used

JAKi, and 792 (13.7%) used oral glucocorticoids.

Mean age was 64.2 years (SD 14.2) among all patients, with a mean of 62.3 years (SD

14.9) for those with breakthrough COVID-19 and 64.6 years (SD 14.0) for those without.  Of the

patients who had breakthrough COVID, 86.6% were White, while 83.6% of patients without

were White. The percent of patients with ILD was 6.3% in those with breakthrough COVID and

5.0% without. Median RA duration was similar at 5 (IQR 2,10) years in both groups. Median

number of healthcare encounters in the previous year was 23 (IQR 6, 41) in those with

breakthrough COVID and 12 (IQR 1, 29) in those without. Approximately three-fourths of

patients (75.2%) received their third vaccine dose before December 16, 2021, when the

Omicron wave started. Patients with vs. without COVID-19 after the index date had a higher CCI

[median 2 (IQR 1,4) vs. 1 (IQR 1,3)] and higher rates of hypertension (50.6% vs. 43.3%),

## DISCUSSION

In this large cohort study of patients with RA, we found that CD20i and glucocorticoid

monotherapy use were associated with higher risk of breakthrough COVID-19 compared to

TNFi after the initial vaccine series of three mRNA doses. These novel findings take into

account the current definition of breakthrough infection after the initial vaccine series, which

includes 3 doses in this vulnerable immunosuppressed population25. Further, we include data

collected during the Omicron wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the relevance of our

findings to the contemporary circulating variants. Our findings emphasize the importance of

prioritizing people with RA using CD20i for risk mitigation strategies, such as additional

vaccinations, behavior modification, and preventive therapies.

Patients with RA have an increased risk of COVID infection, hospitalization, and death

compared to those without RA26, even after vaccination3. The most widely used CD20i,

rituximab, has been shown to be associated with worse COVID-19 outcomes in RA patients in a

large cohort that did not examine breakthrough infections27, and was associated with decreased

rates of positive antibodies after three COVID vaccines28.  The third dose of a COVID vaccine

has been shown to reduce overall rates of breakthrough infection in the general population29

and in immunocompromised individuals without analysis of immunomodulator class30. Key

studies that looked at breakthrough infection have used a definition of two vaccine doses 2,17,31–

33. However, to our knowledge we are the first group to have investigated breakthrough infection

risk by immunomodulator class after 3 vaccine doses in patients with RA. Our study shows that

users of CD20i and glucocorticoid monotherapy have an increased risk of COVID-19 even after

3 vaccine doses.

Decreased immune protection from breakthrough infection is likely related to impaired

immune responses to COVID-19 and other vaccinations observed in CD20i users4,34. Rituximab

use in RA patients decreases humoral responses to influenza vaccination35, and these

responses are worse when the vaccine was given 6 months after administration of rituximab

than when given 6 days before the medication36. In another study of RA patients given

rituximab, B cell mediated responses (pneumococcal polysaccharide and the neoantigen KLH),

but not T cell mediated responses (tetanus toxoid or delayed type hypersensitivity responses to

Candida albicans), were decreased by rituximab use37. The impact of glucocorticoid use on

vaccine immunogenicity is less well understood34.  For example, a study of glucocorticoid use

and influenza vaccination found no impact on antibody titers38.

In addition to their associations with risk of breakthrough COVID-19 infection,

immunomodulator use is also associated with worse acute outcomes of COVID-19. Both CD20i

and glucocorticoid monotherapy use greater than an equivalent of prednisone 10 mg daily have

been associated with higher rates of mortality from COVID-19 in people with systemic

Our study has several strengths. We constructed a large contemporary cohort of

patients with RA using immunomodulators linked to vaccine administration records from

Massachusetts and comprehensive data on covariates. We restricted our analysis to patients

with RA to limit confounding by indication of medications and used propensity score-based

methods to confirm our findings. Unlike previous literature, we focused on participants who have

been infected with COVID-19 at least 2 weeks after they received their third vaccine dose,

which meets the current US CDC definition of breakthrough infection. There are also limitations

to the study. First, we used a rule-based approach to identify RA patients so there may be some

misclassification. However, the positive predictive value of this approach is 90%17, and it would

not be feasible to perform medical record review to confirm RA diagnosis for all patients for a

cohort of this size. Second, administrative data in the EHR was used to identify

immunomodulator medications used by individual participants. It is possible that the participants

may not have been adherent or may have changed therapies or that their therapies may have

been held or adjusted around the time of vaccine dose. Misclassification of the use of

immunomodulators would likely bias towards the null and not explain the findings. Third,

glucocorticoid dose was not available to investigate so we cannot determine if there is a

threshold of glucocorticoid dose associated with breakthrough infection risk. Fourth, we may not

have identified all COVID-19 infections, especially when participants used home rapid antigen

tests that may not have been entered into the medical record, when the infection was mild, or

when the patient was not aware of the infection. This could lead to an underestimate of the

incidence rate. We find it unlikely that this would vary by immunomodulator use group so should

Abstract

Objective: Many individuals with rheumatic disease are at higher risk for severe acute COVID-

19. We aimed to evaluate risk factors for Post-Acute Sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) using an

electronic health record (EHR)-based definition.

Methods: We identified patients with prevalent rheumatic diseases and COVID-19 at Mass

General Brigham. PASC was defined by ICD codes, relevant labs, vital signs, and medications,

at least 30 days following the first COVID-19 infection. Patients were followed until the earliest

of incident PASC, repeat COVID-19 infection, 1 year of follow-up, death, or February 19, 2023.

We used multivariable Cox regression to estimate the association of baseline characteristics

with PASC risk.

Results: Among 2,459 patients (76.37% female, mean age 57.4 years), the most common

incident PASC manifestations were cough (14.56%), dyspnea (12.36%), constipation (11.39%),

and fatigue (10.70%). Serious manifestations including acute coronary disease (4.43%),

thromboembolism (3.09%), hypoxemia (3.09%), stroke (1.75%), and myocarditis (0.12%) were

rare. The Delta wave (aHR 0.63, 95% CI: 0.49-0.82) and Omicron era (aHR 0.50, 95% CI: 0.41-

0.62) were associated with lower risk of PASC than the early pandemic (March 2020-June

2021). Age, obesity, comorbidity burden, race, and hospitalization for acute COVID-19 infection

were associated with greater risk of PASC.

Conclusion: Among patients with rheumatic diseases, following their first COVID-19 infection,

using an EHR-based definition, we found a decreased risk of PASC over calendar time. Aside

from glucocorticoids, no specific immunomodulatory medications were associated with

increased risk, and risk factors were otherwise similar to those seen in the general population.

## Introduction

Patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) often use

immunosuppressive medications that can increase the risk of severe acute outcomes of

coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).[1-5] They are also made more vulnerable by blunted

immune response to the SARS-CoV-2 vaccines.[6-14] Additionally, immune dysregulation and

predisposition to autoantibody formation and fibrosis may also contribute to worse COVID-19

outcomes.[15] Whether SARDs and their treatments contribute to an increased risk of post-acute

sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) is unclear.

“Long Covid,” or PASC has been defined in various ways. Some definitions characterize

PASC as any persistent symptom at a specified duration (e.g., one month, three months, or

other time interval) following acute COVID-19 infection.[16-18] More recent definitions have been

based on the presence of specific patient-reported symptoms.[16,19,20] Some have restricted the

definition to the occurrence of specific severe manifestations such as thrombosis, neuropathy,

new-onset diabetes, or other new chronic comorbidity. Using patient-reported symptoms, we

previously found that approximately 50% of patients with SARDs experience PASC after an

acute COVID-19 infection.[21] Several studies in the general population have evaluated PASC

using an electronic health record (EHR)-based definition. Little is known about the burden and

characteristics of EHR-based definitions of PASC, or its risk factors, in patients with SARDs.

EHR-based definitions of PASC and those based on self-report provide complementary

perspectives on the post-acute consequences of COVID-19. Patient-reported outcomes provide

important insights into the patient experience and frequently capture manifestations of PASC

that clinicians may be unaware of and that are unlikely to be documented in clinical notes or as

encounter claims. In contrast, EHR-based definitions of PASC capture symptoms prompting

medical encounters as well as features that may only be diagnosed by a clinician based on

physical exam, laboratory testing, imaging, and other diagnostics.

## Methods

Study population and SARD patient identification

We performed a retrospective cohort study investigating factors associated with PASC

among patients with SARDs at Mass General Brigham (MGB). MGB is a large, multi-center

healthcare system that includes two tertiary care hospitals (Massachusetts General Hospital

and Brigham and Women’s Hospital), twelve community hospitals, and their associated primary

and specialty outpatient centers in the greater Boston, Massachusetts, area. We identified

people who were seen within MGB who were ≥18 years of age, had a positive test result for

SARS-CoV-2 by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or antigen nasopharyngeal test between

March 1, 2020 and January 18, 2023 using the MGB centralized data warehouse, Research

Patient Data Registry (RPDR), and had a rheumatic disease diagnosis based on International

Classification of Diseases (ICD)-10 code. Diagnosis of a SARD was then confirmed by manual

review of the EHR. This approach has been previously described.[1,3] We also required that

patients have a visit within the MGB healthcare system between one and three years prior to the

index date to identify those with a history of engagement in MGB. The first documented SARS-

CoV-2 infection was used as the index date (Figure 1). This study was approved by the MGB

Institutional Review Board (2020P000833).

Ascertainment of potential risk factors and covariates

Patient demographics, rheumatic disease history, COVID-19 vaccine history, and details

of their acute COVID-19 infection (including date, symptoms, and severity) were ascertained by

manual review of the EHR. Calendar time of acute COVID-19 was divided into three categories:

March 1, 2020 through June 30, 2021 during which the Alpha strain was dominant, July 1-

The primary outcome was PASC, defined by any incident post-acute sequelae with no

particular, ICD-10 codes and prescription medications were ascertained in the one year prior to

COVID-19 infection, and laboratory values and vital signs were ascertained in the five years

Post-acute sequelae were defined by ICD-10 codes, laboratory values (low-density

Categorical variables are presented as number (percentage), and continuous variables

are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median ± interquartile range, as appropriate.

The index date was defined as the date of the first documented infection with SARS-CoV-2.

Patients were followed from 30 days after the index date (to identify features of PASC persisting

We assessed the association of factors of interest among SARD patients with the risk of

PASC using unadjusted and multivariable Cox regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HR)

and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The multivariable model was adjusted for age, sex, CCI,

and vaccination status (unvaccinated or partially vaccinated, fully vaccinated based on the initial

definition of 2 mRNA vaccines or 1 Johnson & Johnson/Janssen vaccine, or additional vaccines

beyond the primary vaccination series), and calendar time as described above. Because

hospitalization due to COVID-19 infection occurs after the index date and may be a mediator of

observed associations, it was not included as a covariate.

## Results

Participant Characteristics

We analyzed 2,459 patients with SARDs and COVID-19 (Table 1). The majority of

patients were female (76.37%). The mean (SD) age at time of COVID-19 was 57.4 (16.6) years

and 1,862 (75.72%) were White. The median (IQR) Charlson Comorbidity Index was 1.0 (1.0-

3.0). The most common SARD category was RA (815, 33.14%), followed by other inflammatory

arthritis (561, 22.81%), SLE (268, 10.90%), giant cell arteritis and/or polymyalgia rheumatica

at the time of COVID-19 were methotrexate (591, 24.03%), antimalarials (540, 21.96%), and

the time of COVID-19 included TNF inhibitors (556, 22.61%) followed by CD20 inhibitors (174,

Baseline factors associated with the risk of PASC

During the follow-up period, there were 441 patients who developed PASC by our

diagnostic criteria. Age (aHR 1.05 per 10 years, 95% CI: 1.02-1.09), obesity (aHR 1.29

compared to normal body mass index, 95% CI: 1.12-1.48 compared to normal weight), greater

comorbidity burden (aHR 1.10 per unit increase in CCI, 95% CI: 1.08-1.12), Black race (aHR

1.35, 95% CI: 1.13-1.62 compared to White race), and hospitalization for acute COVID-19

infection (aHR 1.34 compared to no hospitalization, 95% CI: 1.16-1.56) were associated with

greater risk of PASC (Table 2). Infections occurring during the Delta wave (aHR 0.63, 95% CI:

0.49-0.82) and Omicron era (aHR 0.50, 95% CI: 0.41-0.62) were each associated with lower

risk of PASC than the early pandemic (Figure 3A). There was no association of sex, smoking

status, ethnicity, or vaccination status with risk of PASC in adjusted analyses.

Patients with SLE (aHR 1.44, 95% CI: 1.19-1.74) and AAV (aHR 1.28, 95% CI: 1.01-

1.63) had a higher risk of PASC than patients with RA (Figure 3B). Compared to those

receiving antimalarial monotherapy, patients prescribed TNF inhibitors (aHR 0.72, 95% CI: 0.59-

0.87), IL-6 receptor inhibitors (aHR 0.66, 95% CI: 0.48-0.91), CTLA-4 Ig (aHR 0.59, 95% CI:

0.39-0.93), and methotrexate (aHR 0.78, 95% CI: 0.63-0.96) had a lower risk of PASC. There

was no association of CD20 inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, or other csDMARDs with risk of PASC.

Systemic glucocorticoid use was associated with greater risk of PASC (aHR 1.19, 95% CI: 1.05-

1.34) compared with no use.

## Discussion

In this retrospective cohort study of individuals with SARDs and COVID-19 extending

through the Omicron era, we found that the prevalence of PASC using an EHR-based definition

was high. However, we observed a significant decrease in the risk of PASC over calendar time,

perhaps due to differences in variants and availability of vaccines. Among those with SARDs,

we found higher risk of PASC in those with SLE and AAV compared to those with RA, with the

association of SLE with PASC persisting even after adjusting for specific immunomodulatory

medication use. Certain baseline factors (e.g., age, obesity, comorbidity burden, race,

hospitalization for acute COVID-19 infection) associated with PASC in people with SARDs were

similar to those observed in the general population. Our study is the first to leverage an EHR-

based definition of PASC in people with SARDs. A strength of using an EHR-based definition in

contrast to a definition based solely on patient symptoms is that we are able assess these

clinically relevant endpoints.

There has been particular concern regarding whether people with SARDs may be more

vulnerable to PASC due to immunosuppression, a predisposition to autoimmunity, fibrosis,

have more severe acute COVID-19 infection.[21,25,26] We found high rates of PASC in this

vulnerable population but this burden was not distributed equally across all of the organ systems

in which features of PASC were assessed. Features of PASC affecting the cardiovascular,

pulmonary, and gastrointestinal systems were most commonly observed in this population,

while others, such as the musculoskeletal, dermatologic, and coagulation domains were less

commonly affected. In part, this may reflect the frequency with which some manifestations of

PASC were prevalent in this population prior to their COVID-19 infection. However, this also

highlights important directions for future analyses focused on refining the definition of PASC in

this population and identifying opportunities for intervention.

In the general population, risk factors for PASC have included older age, greater

comorbidity burden, obesity, belonging to a racial or ethnic minority, female sex, and

hospitalization for or more severe acute COVID-19 clinical course.[27-29] Indeed, we found similar

risk factors in this study in patients with rheumatic diseases.[27,30] With regard to rheumatic

disease-specific risk factors for PASC, though studies have found that longer duration of

autoimmune disease may be associated with greater risk, we hypothesized that differences in

immunomodulatory treatments would predispose to different risks of PASC.[26,27,31] However, we

did not find consistent associations of use of certain immunomodulators with PASC as we have

in other studies of COVID-19, particularly in the acute setting.[24] The COVAD study utilized a

questionnaire in patients with SARDs to evaluate the risk of PASC as defined by patient-

reported symptoms and also found no specific risk by DMARD treatment.[27]

We found an association of a diagnosis of SLE and AAV with a higher risk of PASC. One

possible explanation for this finding is that the definition of PASC includes features of these

conditions. Therefore, the observed association suggests that flare in SLE and AAV may be an

important post-acute complication of COVID-19. Indeed, we included patients who were users

of the system prior to the index date, and we excluded features from meeting PASC criteria if

higher proportion with neurologic manifestations in SLE and pulmonary manifestations in AAV

suggest that the rheumatic disease may be flaring given that these organ systems are

frequently affected in these diseases (Supplementary Table 4). Risk of incident SLE and

vasculitis may be greater following COVID-19 infection, but whether COVID-19 exacerbates

underlying rheumatic disease is under-studied.[25,32] Our findings also suggest that the factors

contributing to PASC may differ across diseases. When adjusting for specific

immunomodulatory medication, AAV was no longer significantly associated with PASC,

whereas SLE still was. This suggests that medication use may be a factor in the risk of PASC

among people with AAV but that the pathway to PASC in SLE may be different. Further work is

needed to elucidate the pathways driving an association between COVID-19 and PASC in

people with rheumatic diseases and whether disease flares following infection may be

contributing.

In unadjusted analyses, we found that vaccination was associated with a lower risk of

PASC, as we observed in previous earlier studies of the same cohort and as had been

described elsewhere. This finding did not persist in adjusted analyses but these included

calendar time as a covariate which is closely linked with vaccination status. The improvement in

the risk of PASC over calendar time observed in our study is likely multifactorial and may be

related to differences and decreased virulence of the Omicron variant compared to earlier

strains, increased vaccination over time, the availability of treatments for COVID-19, and other

factors. This finding is consistent with those observed in the general population regarding the

decline in risk of PASC over time.[33] Determining whether PASC may continue to decline over

time and whether emphasis on maintaining up-to-date SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rates over time

may contribute to an ongoing decline in PASC risk moving forward warrants further study.

Our study has multiple strengths. First, we systematically identified a large sample of

people with SARDs and COVID-19 infection, both confirmed by manual medical record review.

Second, due to the combination of comprehensive data from our registry as well as from MGB’s

data warehouse, we were able to ascertain key patient and disease-specific features, including

comorbidities, rheumatic disease and related medications, and details of their COVID-19

infection and vaccination history. Third, we leveraged a comprehensive EHR-based definition of

PASC, encompassing ICD-10 codes, medications, laboratory values, and vital signs. Use of

administrative data is helpful for a population estimate of PASC prevalence and risk factors

since it is not dependent on willingness to participate in a prospective research study and

captures multiple facets of PASC, including symptoms (e.g., fatigue, shortness of breath) and

objective findings (e.g., deep vein thrombosis, diabetes). Fourth, our group has continued to

systematically identify people throughout the pandemic, creating a dataset that encompasses

those with COVID-19 infections ranging from the early pandemic through the recent Omicron

era.

Our study also has limitations. First, our use of an EHR-based definition of PASC did not

require attribution of symptoms to COVID-19 infection. The prevalence of PASC may be

overestimated in our study, though other studies with similar broad definitions, whether EHR or

patient questionnaire based, have also demonstrated prevalence of PASC of >50%. Our study

design required that all patients were actively engaged in the MGB healthcare system to limit

potential for differences by ascertainment. In future studies, alternative study designs that use a

comparator group (e.g., SARD patients without COVID-19 infection, SARD patients following

influenza vaccination, or general population comparators following COVID-19 infection) should

be pursued. Despite this limitation, our study establishes important benchmarks and identifies

directions for future studies of PASC in this vulnerable and under-studied population. Second,

our use of ICD-10 codes as opposed to patient questionnaires has the potential to

underestimate certain criteria (e.g., anosmia, fatigue) that may not be reported to providers.

In summary, we established important benchmarks in the risk of PASC among patients

with rheumatic disease using a comprehensive EHR-based definition. We observed significant

improvements in the risk of PASC over time and that the risk of PASC may vary according to

rheumatic disease. As current treatment for PASC is primarily supportive based on symptoms,

further work elucidating the underlying pathophysiology of PASC will be helpful to identify

potential targeted treatments. Our findings identify important avenues for future investigation,

including determining the attribution of ongoing symptoms to COVID-19 infection, better

elucidating the proportion with severe outcomes (e.g., myocardial infarction, thromboembolism)

following COVID-19 infection, and determining the risk of rheumatic disease flare following

COVID-19 infection.
